en.title: 1-H.1 Picture Join Stories to Ten
en.description: Use a simple picture clue to join two groups and find a total no greater than 10.
learningGoals: Identify the two groups shown or described in a picture story.
Count on or count all to find a total within 10.
Say why the answer matches the story.
en.launch: Imagine a picture mat with red counters on one side and blue counters on the other. Before adding, point to each group and say what it represents.
en.conceptExplanation: On a picture mat, the red counters and blue counters are two little teams joining one game. First notice each team by itself, then count the whole mat. You can count every counter or start with the larger team and count on, but your final number should describe both teams together.

workedExample.prompt: A picture mat shows 4 red counters and 3 blue counters. How many counters are on the mat?
workedExample.reasoning: The two visible parts are 4 and 3. Count on from 4: 5, 6, 7. The total is 7 counters.

guidedPractice: Circle the first group in the picture, then circle the second group.
Write the two numbers before finding the total.
Check by touching each pictured object once.
independentPractice: Draw 2 yellow stars and 6 green stars. Find the total.
Draw 5 blocks and 4 more blocks. Find the total.
Make a picture story with a total of 10.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Counting one object twice when the groups are close together.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Mark each object after counting it once.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Answering with one part instead of the whole.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask: did the story ask for one group or both groups together?

en.exitTicket: Show two picture groups with a total of 9 and explain how you counted.

en.title: 1-H.2 Picture Story Addition Equations
en.description: Turn a picture-based joining story into an addition equation with a total no greater than 10.
learningGoals: Match each picture group to a number in an equation.
Use the plus sign to show joining.
Check that the equation total matches the picture story.
en.launch: Look at a picture story before writing symbols. Say the story in words first: one group, another group, all together.
en.conceptExplanation: After you tell a picture story in words, an addition equation becomes its short math caption. The first addend names one visible part, the second addend names the other part, and the total names the whole picture. Reading the equation aloud should sound like the story you saw.

workedExample.prompt: A picture shows 5 birds on a fence and 2 birds in a tree. Write an addition equation for the total number of birds.
workedExample.reasoning: The picture has parts 5 and 2. Joining them gives 7, so the equation is 5 + 2 = 7.

guidedPractice: Underline the first group and write its number.
Underline the second group and write its number.
Read the whole equation aloud as a story.
independentPractice: Draw 3 flowers and 4 more flowers. Write the equation.
Draw 6 cubes and 1 more cube. Write the equation.
Create a picture with two groups and a total of 10, then write the equation.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Writing only the total without the two parts.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Use three blanks: part + part = whole.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Putting a part after the equals sign.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask which number tells how many in all.

en.exitTicket: Write an equation for a picture with 4 dots and 5 dots.

en.title: 1-H.3 Cube-Train Join Models to Ten
en.description: Use a cube-train model to represent two joined parts and find a total within 10.
learningGoals: Build two parts in one train using different colors or labels.
Connect the model to a joining story.
Count the train to find the total within 10.
en.launch: Pretend each cube is a counter in the story. Build the first part, then snap on the second part before counting the whole train.
en.conceptExplanation: A cube train keeps the story in your hands. One color shows the first part, another color shows the second part, and the snapped-together train shows the whole. The color break is a bookmark: it reminds you where one part ends while you count the total.

workedExample.prompt: A cube train has 6 green cubes and 2 yellow cubes. How many cubes are in the train?
workedExample.reasoning: The model shows 6 cubes joined with 2 cubes. Count on from 6: 7, 8. The train has 8 cubes.

guidedPractice: Build the first part before adding the second part.
Point to the color break and name the two addends.
Count all cubes once to check the total.
independentPractice: Build 4 cubes and 4 cubes. Write the total.
Build 7 cubes and 3 cubes. Write the total.
Build a cube train for your own story with a total less than 10.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Losing track of the two parts after snapping the train together.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Use two colors or place a small marker at the join.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Starting the count over after the first part but skipping the second part.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Either count every cube or count on from the first part.

en.exitTicket: Describe a cube train for 3 + 5 and give the total.

en.title: 1-H.4 Join Stories Within Ten
en.description: Solve a joining story without relying on a picture, keeping the total no greater than 10.
learningGoals: Listen for two amounts that are being joined.
Choose counting on, drawing, or an equation to solve.
Explain the total in the context of the story.
en.launch: Some joining stories are told only with words. Make a quick sketch or finger model if you need to see the parts.
en.conceptExplanation: A word story can be pictured in your mind even when no drawing is given. Listen for the two amounts that are being put together, then choose a quick sketch, fingers, or counting on to find the whole. The answer should tell how many there are in all.

workedExample.prompt: Leo reads 3 pages before lunch and 5 pages after lunch. How many pages does Leo read in all?
workedExample.reasoning: The story joins 3 pages and 5 pages. 3 + 5 = 8, so Leo reads 8 pages.

guidedPractice: Tell which two amounts are being joined.
Choose a strategy before you solve.
Write the answer with a label from the story.
independentPractice: Nina plants 2 seeds and then 7 more seeds. Find the total.
A tray has 6 cups and gets 3 more cups. Find the total.
Write your own joining story with total 10.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Using subtraction because the story has the word after or before.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask whether the story keeps both amounts together.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Forgetting the unit in the answer.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Copy the object name from the question into the answer sentence.

en.exitTicket: Solve: Sam has 4 shells and finds 6 more. Explain your strategy.

en.title: 1-H.5 Model-and-Equation Join Stories
en.description: Represent a joining story with a model and an addition equation, with totals no greater than 10.
learningGoals: Create a model for each part of a joining story.
Translate the model into an addition equation.
Use the model to check the equation.
en.launch: Before writing numbers, show the story with quick circles, tally marks, fingers, or counters.
en.conceptExplanation: Think of the model as the movie of the story and the equation as the title card. If the model shows 4 shells and 5 more shells joining, the equation should record those same parts and the same whole. When the model and equation agree, your answer has a reason.

workedExample.prompt: A basket has 4 apples. Then 5 more apples are added. Model the story and write the equation.
workedExample.reasoning: Draw 4 counters, then 5 more counters. Counting all counters gives 9, so the matching equation is 4 + 5 = 9.

guidedPractice: Draw or build the first part.
Draw or build the second part.
Write the equation in the same order as the model.
independentPractice: Model and write an equation for 2 balloons and 6 more balloons.
Model and write an equation for 5 pencils and 4 more pencils.
Create a story, model, and equation for a total of 10.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: The model shows one story but the equation shows another.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Point from each group in the model to its number in the equation.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Writing the plus sign before naming both parts.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Say part, part, whole before writing symbols.

en.exitTicket: Draw a model for 6 + 3 and explain how it matches the equation.

en.title: 1-H.6 Equation Match for Join Stories
en.description: Choose or write the addition equation that matches a joining story within 10.
learningGoals: Identify the two addends in a story.
Match the story to an equation with the correct total.
Use the equals sign to show that both sides name the same amount.
en.launch: Read the whole story before choosing an equation. The numbers alone are not enough; the operation must match the action.
en.conceptExplanation: An equation is true only if it tells the same joining story. Different number sentences may have the same total, but the best match uses the exact two parts from the story. Read the story, point to each part, then choose the equation that makes the picture and words agree.

workedExample.prompt: A tank has 2 orange fish and 6 silver fish. Which equation matches the total number of fish?
workedExample.reasoning: The story joins 2 fish and 6 fish. The total is 8, so 2 + 6 = 8 matches the story.

guidedPractice: Cross out equations that use the wrong operation.
Check that both story parts appear in the equation.
Read the equation as a sentence and compare it to the story.
independentPractice: Match a story about 1 red cup and 8 blue cups to an equation.
Match a story about 5 small rocks and 5 large rocks to an equation.
Write two true equations and explain which one matches the story order.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Choosing an equation only because it has the same total.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Check that the addends also match the two story parts.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Treating the equals sign as a signal to calculate instead of a balance.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Read equals as 'is the same amount as'.

en.exitTicket: Write the matching equation for a story with 3 red cubes and 4 blue cubes.

en.title: 1-L.1 Picture Take-Away Stories to Ten
en.description: Use a simple picture clue to remove a part and find how many remain within 10.
learningGoals: Identify the starting amount in a picture story.
Identify the part that is taken away.
Count what remains within 10.
en.launch: Picture stories for subtraction usually show a starting group and a change. Before solving, name what was there first and what left.
en.conceptExplanation: A take-away picture has a before and an after. The whole group is there first, then some objects leave, get used, or are crossed out. The answer is the part still left in the picture, not the part that went away.

workedExample.prompt: A picture shows 9 balloons. Four balloons float away. How many balloons are left?
workedExample.reasoning: Start with 9 balloons and remove 4. Counting back or crossing out 4 leaves 5 balloons.

guidedPractice: Box the starting group in the picture.
Cross out or cover the part that leaves.
Count the part that remains.
independentPractice: Draw 8 apples and cross out 3. Find how many remain.
Draw 6 cups and remove 2. Find how many remain.
Create a take-away picture with 10 objects.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Adding the removed part instead of subtracting it.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask whether the group grows or gets smaller.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Counting the crossed-out objects as the answer.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Point to what is left and count only those objects.

en.exitTicket: Draw a picture for 7 take away 2 and say how many remain.

en.title: 1-L.2 Picture Story Subtraction Equations
en.description: Turn a picture-based take-away story into a subtraction equation within 10.
learningGoals: Match the starting picture amount to the first number.
Match the removed part to the number after the minus sign.
Check that the equation's result is the amount left.
en.launch: Say the picture story with subtraction language: start with, take away, left.
en.conceptExplanation: A subtraction equation is a short record of a take-away story. The first number names the starting whole, the second number names the part removed, and the answer names what remains. If you read the equation aloud, it should sound like start, take away, left.

workedExample.prompt: A picture shows 8 crackers. Three crackers are eaten. Write a subtraction equation for how many crackers are left.
workedExample.reasoning: The story starts with 8 and removes 3. Five remain, so the equation is 8 - 3 = 5.

guidedPractice: Write the starting number first.
Write the removed number after the minus sign.
Read the equation back as a story.
independentPractice: Draw 7 beads and remove 4. Write the equation.
Draw 10 dots and remove 6. Write the equation.
Create a picture and subtraction equation with an answer of 3.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Putting the smaller number first because it looks easier.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: The first number must be the starting whole in the story.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Writing the removed part as the answer.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask how many are still there after the change.

en.exitTicket: Write the equation for 9 toys with 2 toys taken away.

en.title: 1-L.3 Cube-Train Take-Away Models to Ten
en.description: Use a cube train to model taking away a part and finding what remains within 10.
learningGoals: Build the starting amount as one cube train.
Remove or cover the part taken away.
Count the cubes that remain.
en.launch: Build the whole train first. Then slide away or cover the part that leaves so the remaining part is easy to see.
en.conceptExplanation: For subtraction, build the whole cube train before anything leaves. When you slide away or cover some cubes, the hidden or moved part shows the take-away action. The cubes still showing are the answer because they are the part left behind.

workedExample.prompt: A cube train has 10 cubes. Six cubes are covered. How many cubes can you still see?
workedExample.reasoning: Start with 10 cubes and cover 6. The visible part is 4 cubes, so 10 - 6 = 4.

guidedPractice: Build the whole train before removing anything.
Count the removed or covered cubes.
Count the visible or remaining cubes to answer.
independentPractice: Build 9 cubes and cover 5. Find what remains.
Build 7 cubes and remove 3. Find what remains.
Build a cube-train story with an answer of 2.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Building only the removed part instead of the starting whole.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: The train starts with the first number in the story.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Counting covered cubes as the answer.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Choose whether the question asks for covered cubes or visible cubes.

en.exitTicket: Explain how a 9-cube train can show 9 - 4.

en.title: 1-L.4 Take-Away Stories Within Ten
en.description: Solve a take-away story without relying on a picture, using totals no greater than 10.
learningGoals: Identify the starting amount and the amount removed.
Choose a subtraction strategy such as counting back, drawing, or using a related addition fact.
Answer with the amount left in the story.
en.launch: When a story says some objects are used, given away, eaten, or leave, ask whether the group gets smaller.
en.conceptExplanation: In a take-away story, the group starts with a full amount and then gets smaller. Words like gave away, ate, used, or left can signal a change, but the story is more important than a keyword. Ask what stayed, because the leftover part is the answer.

workedExample.prompt: Tara has 7 stickers. She gives 2 stickers to a friend. How many stickers does Tara have left?
workedExample.reasoning: Tara starts with 7 and gives away 2. Count back 2 from 7: 6, 5. Tara has 5 stickers left.

guidedPractice: Name the starting amount.
Name the amount that leaves.
Use the story label in the final answer.
independentPractice: A box has 8 crayons. Three are used. Find how many are left.
A shelf has 10 books. Four are checked out. Find how many are left.
Write your own take-away story with an answer of 6.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Using the first two numbers in any order.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Keep the starting whole first in a take-away story.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Stopping the count-back one step too soon.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Count the jumps, not just the number words.

en.exitTicket: Solve: 9 markers, 5 are put away. How many are still out?

en.title: 1-L.5 Model-and-Equation Take-Away Stories
en.description: Represent a take-away story with a model and a subtraction equation within 10.
learningGoals: Model the starting amount before showing the change.
Show the removed part by crossing out, covering, or moving objects.
Write a subtraction equation that matches the model.
en.launch: A strong subtraction model shows the whole first. Then it shows exactly what changed.
en.conceptExplanation: The model is the proof for the subtraction equation. If the model starts with 9 counters and 5 are crossed out, the equation must start with 9 and subtract 5. The leftover counters and the answer in the equation should match.

workedExample.prompt: Draw 9 counters. Cross out 5 counters. Write an equation for how many counters are left.
workedExample.reasoning: The model starts with 9 counters and removes 5. Four counters are not crossed out, so the equation is 9 - 5 = 4.

guidedPractice: Draw or build the starting whole.
Show the part taken away without erasing the whole.
Write the equation and point to each part of the model.
independentPractice: Model and write an equation for 8 - 6.
Model and write an equation for 10 - 3.
Create a take-away story, model, and equation with an answer of 5.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Erasing the removed objects so the starting whole is no longer visible.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Cross out or cover instead of erasing.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Writing an equation that does not match the model.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Point from the whole, removed part, and leftover part to the equation.

en.exitTicket: Model 6 - 2 and write one sentence explaining the equation.

en.title: 1-L.6 Break-Apart Subtraction Equations
en.description: Write and solve a subtraction equation for a story where a whole is separated into parts within 10.
learningGoals: Identify the whole and the known part in a take-apart story.
Use subtraction to find the missing part.
Check with a related addition fact.
en.launch: Not every subtraction story has objects leaving. Sometimes the whole is split into two parts and one part is unknown.
en.conceptExplanation: Sometimes subtraction is a hidden-part story instead of a leaving story. The whole is known, one part is known, and the other part is missing. Subtracting the known part from the whole uncovers the missing part, like lifting a flap on the picture.

workedExample.prompt: There are 10 shells. Four shells are in a box, and the rest are on the table. How many shells are on the table?
workedExample.reasoning: The whole is 10 shells. One part is 4 shells in the box. The missing part is 10 - 4 = 6, so 6 shells are on the table.

guidedPractice: Label the whole before writing an equation.
Label the known part.
Use addition to check that the two parts make the whole.
independentPractice: There are 8 buttons. Three are red and the rest are blue. Find the blue buttons.
There are 9 cubes. Five are tall-stack cubes and the rest are flat. Find the flat cubes.
Write a break-apart story for 7 - 2.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Thinking subtraction always means something leaves.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Use whole-part-part language for break-apart stories.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Subtracting the missing part instead of the known part.
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Name what is known before choosing the equation.

en.exitTicket: Solve: 9 counters are split into 6 red counters and some blue counters. How many are blue?
